'''Nicholas Wright Gillham''' (May 14, 1932 – March 19, 2018) was an American geneticist who served as the [[James B. Duke]] Professor of [[Biology]] at [[Duke University]]. In addition to his scientific research, he is known for his 2001 [[biography]] of [[Francis Galton]], ''A Life of Sir Francis Galton: From African Exploration to the Birth of Eugenics''.

==Early life and education==
Gillham was born on May 14, 1932, in [[New York City]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. His father, Robert Marty Gillham, was an advertising executive, and his mother, [[Elizabeth Enright]], was a writer of children's books and the niece of the architect [[Frank Lloyd Wright]]. He received his [[Ph.D.]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1962, and completed his [[postdoc]] at [[Yale University]] from 1961 to 1963.<ref name="legacy">{{Cite news |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/heraldsun/obituary.aspx?n=nicholas-wright-gillham&pid=188563206 |title=Nicholas Wright Gillham |date=2018-03-27 |work=Herald Sun |access-date=2019-08-01}}</ref>

==Academic career==
After serving as an instructor and later as assistant professor at Harvard, Gillham joined the faculty of Duke University in 1968, where he was named James B. Duke Professor in 1982. He served as chair of the Department of Zoology at Duke from 1986 to 1989. He would remain on the faculty at Duke until his retirement in 2002.<ref name="legacy"/><ref name="today">{{Cite web |url=https://today.duke.edu/2018/03/duke-flags-lowered-nicholas-gillham-leading-duke-geneticist-dies-age-85 |title=Duke Flags Lowered: Nicholas Gillham, Leading Duke Geneticist, Dies at Age 85 |date=2018-03-22 |website=Duke Today |language=en |access-date=2019-08-01}}</ref> He was a member of the President's Biomedical Research Panel in 1975 and a member of the [[National Institute of Health]]'s study section in genetics from 1976 to 1980, as well as a [[senior editor]] of the journal ''Plasmid'' from 1977 to 1986.<ref name="contemporary"/>

==Books==
Gillham wrote three technical books during his career: one about [[microbiology]] and two about the [[genetics]] of [[organelles]].<ref name="today"/> In 2001, he published the book ''A Life of Sir Francis Galton: From African Exploration to the Birth of Eugenics'', a biography of [[Francis Galton]]. A review of this book in ''[[Publishers Weekly]]'' stated that "[t]his may well prove to be the definitive biography" of Galton.<ref>{{Cite magazine |title=A LIFE OF SIR FRANCIS GALTON: From African Explorer to the Birth of Eugenics |url=https://www.publishersweekly.com/9780195143652 |magazine=Publishers Weekly |access-date=2019-08-01}}</ref> Similarly, [[Theodore M. Porter]] reviewed the book favorably, describing it in the journal ''[[Isis (journal)|Isis]]'' as "a sound, readable account that will become, for most, the Galton biography of choice."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Porter |first=Theodore M. |date=September 2002 |title=Nicholas Wright Gillham. A Life of Sir Francis Galton: From African Exploration to the Birth of Eugenics . 416 pp., illus., figs., notes, bibl., index. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001. $30 (cloth). |magazine=Isis |language=en |volume=93 |issue=3 |pages=491–492 |doi=10.1086/374096 |issn=0021-1753}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Gillham received a Research Career Development Award from 1972 to 1977<ref name="contemporary">{{Cite encyclopedia |title=Gillham, Nicholas Wright 1932- |encyclopedia=Contemporary Authors |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/gillham-nicholas-wright-1932 |access-date=2019-08-01 |year=2009}}</ref> and a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1984.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/nicholas-wright-gillham/ |title=Nicholas Wright Gillham |website=John Simon Guggenheim Foundation |language=en-US |access-date=2019-08-01}}</ref> He was also a member of the [[Genetics Society of America]].<ref name="contemporary"/>

==Personal life and death==
Gillham married Carol Lenore Collins on June 2, 1956.<ref name="contemporary"/> They remained married until Gillham's death. Gillham died of a [[heart attack]] at his home in [[Fearrington Village, North Carolina]], on March 19, 2018.<ref name="legacy"/>
